LPS Final Memo Lab & Citation Suite

Focused strictly on your Dec 17 closed-universe memo: Smoothie Rule Synthesis, CREAC Architecture, Targeted Fixes & Bluebook Citations.

Closed-Universe Memo Architecture
1. Heading & Question Presented (1 sentence): "Under [governing statute/law], does [legal issue] apply when [3–4 legally dispositive facts by role, no proper names], but [key contrary fact]?" (Zero case names in QP).
2. Brief Answer (1 paragraph): Lead with "Likely yes." or "Probably not." → broad rule → mini-application with "because" (zero case names or citations).
3. Discussion (Umbrella + CREAC): Umbrella clears undisputed elements in 1 sentence. Rule (R) puts statute first, then blends cases into one unified rule ("smoothie", never case-by-case "parfait"), with citations at the end of every sentence. Explanation (E) opens each paragraph with a standalone sub-rule thesis + FHR (Facts, Holding, Reasoning) + specific policy. Application (A) opens with a parallel client thesis (NO case names, NO citations in A), compares critical facts + reasoning, resolves counterarguments in an "Although" sentence, and concludes with "will likely".

Interactive Rule Synthesis Builder ("Smoothie, Not Parfait")

Packet cases on Georgia's shopkeeper's privilege (reasonable manner of detention):
• Mitchell: Guard searched shopper's bag in open store for 10–15 mins without touching shopper or accusing her → Reasonable.
• Brown: Employee grabbed shopper's arm, slung her, and shoved her into candy rack → Unreasonable.
• Jackson: Loss-prevention manager made personal racial/sexual remarks unrelated to theft investigation → Unreasonable.

Model Synthesized Rule:
Georgia's shopkeeper's privilege requires reasonable belief, reasonable time, and reasonable manner of detention. Ga. Code Ann. § 51-7-60. Only the manner is at issue here. A detention is unreasonable in manner when store personnel subject the shopper to gratuitous and unnecessary indignities, either through physical contact beyond a casual touching or through personal remarks unrelated to the theft investigation. Brown v. Super Disc. Mkts., Inc., 477 S.E.2d 839, 840–41 (Ga. Ct. App. 1996); Jackson v. Kmart Corp., 851 F. Supp. 469, [add pin cite from your packet] (M.D. Ga. 1994). Conduct causing mere embarrassment without more does not make a detention unreasonable. Mitchell v. Walmart Stores, Inc., 477 S.E.2d 631, 633 (Ga. Ct. App. 1996).

Case Citation Builder

Bluebook & Memo Citation Checker

Paste a citation or sentence to check for common rubric deductions ("Id." after string cites, "at" in full cites, starting sentences with statutory abbreviations, or "Ibid.").

High-Value Rubric Checklist (Before Turning In Your Dec 17 Final)
1. Rule Section: Never open a sentence with "O.C.G.A. §" or numbers (write "Section..." or name the privilege). State ALL statutory elements first before narrowing to the disputed element. Blend cases into one "smoothie" rule at the category level, with citations at the end of every sentence.
2. Explanation (E): Open every E paragraph with a standalone sub-rule thesis (never "The same breakdown..." or "In [Case]..."). Group all cases for a sub-rule together (FHR + specific policy grounded in the court's reasoning).
3. Application (A): Open with a parallel client thesis (NO case names in the thesis). Include ZERO citations anywhere in A (use underlined short case names like Mitchell). Put every fact under its matching sub-rule.
4. Predictions & Citations: Replace hedged verbs ("may", "could", "might", "could be inclined") with "will likely" / "probably not". Never use "Id." after a string citation, and always include pinpoint pages.
